/-!
# In parallelohedron: the Voronoi conjecture

A *parallelohedron* (or *parallelotope*) is a convex $d$-dimensional polytope $P$ that tiles
$\mathbb{R}^d$ by translated copies of itself. The Dirichlet–Voronoi cell of a lattice
$\Lambda \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ (the set of points at least as close to the origin as to any other
lattice point) is always a parallelohedron. The **Voronoi conjecture** asserts the converse up to
affine transformations: every parallelohedron is an affine image of the Dirichlet–Voronoi cell of
some lattice.

For $d = 3$ this says that every parallelohedron can be made into a plesiohedron (here, the Voronoi
cell of a lattice) by an affine transformation. Delaunay proved this in 1929 for $d = 3$ and
$d = 4$, Garber proved it for $d = 5$, and it is open for $d \ge 6$.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia: Parallelohedron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/parallelohedron)
- [Wikipedia: List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [arXiv:1906.05193](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.05193), A. Garber, *Voronoi conjecture for
  five-dimensional parallelohedra*.
-/

blocks.docstring:
A set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ *tiles $\mathbb{R}^d$ by translations* if there is a set $T$ of
translation vectors such that the translates $t + P$, $t \in T$, cover $\mathbb{R}^d$ and have
pairwise disjoint interiors.

justification.closest_existing_considered: `tilesByTranslation` in FormalConjecturesForMathlib/Analysis/Fourier/SpectralSets.lean — defined on `Fin d → ℝ` (not Euclidean) and measure-theoretically, so it does not combine with the Euclidean Voronoi cell; also `MeasureTheory.IsAddFundamentalDomain` (measure-theoretic, lattice-specific).
justification.name: InParallelohedron.TilesByTranslations
justification.why_needed: Geometric notion of a set tiling ℝ^d by translates (covering with pairwise disjoint interiors) on `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)`; Mathlib has no tiling notion.

blocks.name: TilesByTranslations
blocks.text:
/-- A set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ *tiles $\mathbb{R}^d$ by translations* if there is a set $T$ of
translation vectors such that the translates $t + P$, $t \in T$, cover $\mathbb{R}^d$ and have
pairwise disjoint interiors. -/
def TilesByTranslations (P : Set (ℝ^d)) : Prop :=
  ∃ T : Set (ℝ^d), (⋃ t ∈ T, t +ᵥ P) = Set.univ ∧
    T.Pairwise fun s t => Disjoint (interior (s +ᵥ P)) (interior (t +ᵥ P))

blocks.code:
def IsParallelohedron (P : Set (ℝ^d)) : Prop :=
  (∃ S : Finset (ℝ^d), P = convexHull ℝ ↑S) ∧ (interior P).Nonempty ∧ TilesByTranslations P
blocks.docstring:
A *parallelohedron* in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is a $d$-dimensional convex polytope, i.e. the convex hull
of a finite set of points with nonempty interior, that tiles $\mathbb{R}^d$ by translations.
The nonempty interior condition expresses that the polytope is genuinely $d$-dimensional.

justification.closest_existing_considered: `convexHull ℝ (S : Finset _)` with `(interior _).Nonempty`, as used in FormalConjectures/Paper/Rupert.lean; used as the building block.
justification.name: InParallelohedron.IsParallelohedron
justification.why_needed: Convex d-polytope (finite convex hull with nonempty interior) that tiles ℝ^d by translations; Mathlib has no convex polytope or parallelohedron notion.

blocks.name: IsParallelohedron
blocks.text:
/-- A *parallelohedron* in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is a $d$-dimensional convex polytope, i.e. the convex hull
of a finite set of points with nonempty interior, that tiles $\mathbb{R}^d$ by translations.
The nonempty interior condition expresses that the polytope is genuinely $d$-dimensional. -/
def IsParallelohedron (P : Set (ℝ^d)) : Prop :=

blocks.code:
def dirichletVoronoiCell (Λ : Set (ℝ^d)) : Set (ℝ^d) :=
  {x | ∀ l ∈ Λ, dist x 0 ≤ dist x l}
blocks.docstring:
The (closed) *Dirichlet–Voronoi cell* of the origin with respect to a set
$\Lambda \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$: the points of $\mathbb{R}^d$ that are at least as close to $0$ as
to any point of $\Lambda$. When $\Lambda$ is a lattice, this is the Dirichlet–Voronoi polytope of
$\Lambda$.

justification.name: InParallelohedron.dirichletVoronoiCell
justification.why_needed: Closed Dirichlet–Voronoi cell of a set (in particular a lattice) at the origin; Mathlib has no Voronoi cell/diagram definition (only a doc mention in MeasureTheory/Group/GeometryOfNumbers.lean).

def VoronoiConjectureDim (d : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ P : Set (ℝ^d), IsParallelohedron P →
    ∃ (Λ : Submodule ℤ (ℝ^d)) (_ : DiscreteTopology Λ) (_ : IsZLattice ℝ Λ) (A : ℝ^d ≃ᵃ[ℝ] ℝ^d),
      A '' P = dirichletVoronoiCell Λ
blocks.docstring:
The **Voronoi conjecture** in dimension $d$: for every parallelohedron $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$
there exist a full-rank lattice $\Lambda \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and an affine transformation
$\mathcal{A}$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ such that $\mathcal{A}(P)$ is the Dirichlet–Voronoi cell of
$\Lambda$.

justification.closest_existing_considered: None; analogous to `Kakeya.KakeyaSetConjectureDim` and `Fuglede.FugledeConjectureFor` in the repository.
justification.name: InParallelohedron.VoronoiConjectureDim
justification.why_needed: The dimension-d instance of the Voronoi conjecture, so that the open statement and the solved low-dimensional variants share one formulation.

blocks.name: VoronoiConjectureDim
blocks.text:
/-- The **Voronoi conjecture** in dimension $d$: for every parallelohedron $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$
there exist a full-rank lattice $\Lambda \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and an affine transformation
$\mathcal{A}$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ such that $\mathcal{A}(P)$ is the Dirichlet–Voronoi cell of
$\Lambda$. -/
def VoronoiConjectureDim (d : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ P : Set (ℝ^d), IsParallelohedron P →
    ∃ (Λ : Submodule ℤ (ℝ^d)) (_ : DiscreteTopology Λ) (_ : IsZLattice ℝ Λ) (A : ℝ^d ≃ᵃ[ℝ] ℝ^d),
      A '' P = dirichletVoronoiCell Λ

claims.decomposer_note: Statement is a bare list heading, so the question is taken from the article; the polyhedron need not be convex (only its boundary must be a 2-sphere), the tiling is by translations only, and 'patches' are connected unions of faces whose incidence structure must equal the face lattice of one of the five Fedorov types (parallelepiped, hexagonal prism, rhombic dodecahedron, elongated dodecahedron, truncated octahedron).
claims.reviewer_why: Omitted. Grünbaum's conjecture as rendered on Wikipedia is informal: it does not fix what a (non-convex) 'polyhedron with faces' is, what 'connected' means for a set of faces (edge- vs vertex-connected), or what 'the same combinatorial structure' means (intersection-poset isomorphism vs. cell-complex/topological equivalence). Only c02 and c08 attempted it, and they embody materially different, non-equivalent readings: c02 requires disc faces, forbids coplanar edge-adjacent faces, restricts face intersections to ∅/point/segment (excluding legitimate translational tiles with annular faces or faces meeting in a segment plus a point) and uses edge-connectivity; c08 requires convex faces, allows arbitrary coplanar subdivisions (so patches may cut across true faces, weakening the conjecture for polyhedra with non-convex faces) and uses topological connectivity. Each restricts or alters the hypothesis class in ways the source does not support, and I could not produce a formulation robust to these ambiguities. Six of eight candidates (c01, c03, c04, c05, c06, c07) omitted this slot for these reasons; I agree with them.
claims.source_text: According to a conjecture of Branko Grünbaum, for every polyhedron that is topologically a sphere and can tile space by translation, it is possible to group its faces into patches (unions of connected subsets of faces) so that the combinatorial structure of these patches is the same as the combinatorial structure of the faces of one of the five Federov parallelohedra. This conjecture remains unproven.
claims.text_span: According to a conjecture of Branko Grünbaum, for every polyhedron that is topologically a sphere and can tile space by translation, it is possible to group its faces into patches (unions of connected subsets of faces) so that the combinatorial structure of these patches is the same as the combinatorial structure of the faces of one of the five Federov parallelohedra. This conjecture remains unproven.

claims.decomposer_note: This is the Voronoi conjecture (precise form in cited arXiv:1906.05193): for every d and every convex d-polytope P tiling ℝ^d by translations there exist a lattice Λ and an affine map A with A(P) the Dirichlet–Voronoi cell of Λ; it is known for d ≤ 5 and open for d ≥ 6, and for convex translational tiles one may assume the tiling is a face-to-face lattice tiling without loss.
claims.reviewer_why: States the Voronoi conjecture exactly in Garber's form (arXiv:1906.05193): for every d and every parallelohedron P ⊆ ℝ^d (convex hull of a finite set with nonempty interior tiling ℝ^d by translations — cover by translates with pairwise disjoint interiors, no face-to-face assumption, as in the source), there exist a full-rank lattice Λ (Mathlib's `Submodule ℤ` with `DiscreteTopology` and `IsZLattice ℝ`) and an affine equivalence A with A(P) the closed Euclidean Dirichlet–Voronoi cell of Λ at the origin. Ambient space is `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)` so `dist` is Euclidean. The d = 0 instance is trivially true and harmless. c05 also records the text span's solved cases (d = 3, 4 by Delaunay; d = 5 by Garber; d ≤ 5) as `research solved` variants via a reusable `VoronoiConjectureDim d`. c03, c04, c06, c07 are equally faithful; c05 was chosen for its clean structure and variants. c01, c02, c08 were rejected for this slot because they work in `Fin d → ℝ`, whose `dist` is the sup metric, so their 'Voronoi cell' is not the Euclidean Dirichlet–Voronoi cell and the statement is a different (wrong) conjecture. Only docstrings were lightly edited.
claims.source_text: However, as Boris Delaunay proved in 1929, every parallelohedron can be made into a plesiohedron by an affine transformation. He also proved the same fact for four-dimensional parallelohedra, and it has been proven as well for five dimensions, but this remains open in higher dimensions.

He also proved the same fact for four-dimensional parallelohedra, and it has been proven as well for five dimensions, but this remains open in higher dimensions.

context:
In geometry, a parallelohedron or Fedorov polyhedron is a convex polyhedron that can be translated without rotations to fill Euclidean space, producing a honeycomb in which all copies of the polyhedron meet face-to-face. Evgraf Fedorov identified the five types of parallelohedron in 1885 in his studies of crystallographic systems. They are the cube, hexagonal prism, rhombic dodecahedron, elongated dodecahedron, and truncated octahedron.
Each parallelohedron is centrally symmetric with symmetric faces, making it a special case of a zonohedron. Each parallelohedron is also a stereohedron, a polyhedron that tiles space so that all tiles are symmetric. The centers of the tiles in a tiling of space by parallelohedra form a Bravais lattice, and every Bravais lattice can be formed in this way. Adjusting the lengths of parallel edges in a parallelohedron, or performing an affine transformation of the  parallelohedron, results in another parallelohedron of the same combinatorial type. It is possible to choose this adjustment so that the tiling by parallelohedra is the Voronoi diagram of its Bravais lattice, and so that the resulting parallelohedra become special cases of the plesiohedra. 
The three-dimensional parallelohedra are analogous to two-dimensional parallelogons and higher-dimensional parallelotopes.

decomposition_objections.text: No objection to the split. One remark on slot i: the note's reading that the patch incidence structure 'must equal the face lattice' of a Fedorov type is a reasonable but not the only possible reading of Grünbaum's informal phrase 'combinatorial structure of these patches' (it could also be read as the patch adjacency structure only); this ambiguity, on top of the missing primitives, is part of why slot i was not stated. For slot ii, the note's remark that one may assume a face-to-face lattice tiling is correct but not needed: the formalization uses the general (not necessarily face-to-face) tiling definition, exactly as Garber's paper does.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# In parallelohedron: the Voronoi conjecture

A *parallelohedron* (or *parallelotope*) is a convex $d$-dimensional polytope $P$ that tiles
$\mathbb{R}^d$ by translated copies of itself. The Dirichlet–Voronoi cell of a lattice
$\Lambda \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ (the set of points at least as close to the origin as to any other
lattice point) is always a parallelohedron. The **Voronoi conjecture** asserts the converse up to
affine transformations: every parallelohedron is an affine image of the Dirichlet–Voronoi cell of
some lattice.

For $d = 3$ this says that every parallelohedron can be made into a plesiohedron (here, the Voronoi
cell of a lattice) by an affine transformation. Delaunay proved this in 1929 for $d = 3$ and
$d = 4$, Garber proved it for $d = 5$, and it is open for $d \ge 6$.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia: Parallelohedron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/parallelohedron)
- [Wikipedia: List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [arXiv:1906.05193](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.05193), A. Garber, *Voronoi conjecture for
  five-dimensional parallelohedra*.
-/

open scoped EuclideanGeometry Pointwise

namespace InParallelohedron

variable {d : ℕ}

/-- A set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ *tiles $\mathbb{R}^d$ by translations* if there is a set $T$ of
translation vectors such that the translates $t + P$, $t \in T$, cover $\mathbb{R}^d$ and have
pairwise disjoint interiors. -/
def TilesByTranslations (P : Set (ℝ^d)) : Prop :=
  ∃ T : Set (ℝ^d), (⋃ t ∈ T, t +ᵥ P) = Set.univ ∧
    T.Pairwise fun s t => Disjoint (interior (s +ᵥ P)) (interior (t +ᵥ P))

/-- A *parallelohedron* in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is a $d$-dimensional convex polytope, i.e. the convex hull
of a finite set of points with nonempty interior, that tiles $\mathbb{R}^d$ by translations.
The nonempty interior condition expresses that the polytope is genuinely $d$-dimensional. -/
def IsParallelohedron (P : Set (ℝ^d)) : Prop :=
  (∃ S : Finset (ℝ^d), P = convexHull ℝ ↑S) ∧ (interior P).Nonempty ∧ TilesByTranslations P

/-- The (closed) *Dirichlet–Voronoi cell* of the origin with respect to a set
$\Lambda \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$: the points of $\mathbb{R}^d$ that are at least as close to $0$ as
to any point of $\Lambda$. When $\Lambda$ is a lattice, this is the Dirichlet–Voronoi polytope of
$\Lambda$. -/
def dirichletVoronoiCell (Λ : Set (ℝ^d)) : Set (ℝ^d) :=
  {x | ∀ l ∈ Λ, dist x 0 ≤ dist x l}

/-- The origin lies in every Dirichlet–Voronoi cell of the origin. -/
@[category API, AMS 52]
theorem zero_mem_dirichletVoronoiCell (Λ : Set (ℝ^d)) : 0 ∈ dirichletVoronoiCell Λ := by
  simp [dirichletVoronoiCell]

/-- The Dirichlet–Voronoi cell with respect to the empty set is the whole space. -/
@[category API, AMS 52]
theorem dirichletVoronoiCell_empty : dirichletVoronoiCell (∅ : Set (ℝ^d)) = Set.univ := by
  simp [dirichletVoronoiCell]

/-- The whole space tiles itself by translations. -/
@[category test, AMS 52]
theorem tilesByTranslations_univ : TilesByTranslations (Set.univ : Set (ℝ^d)) := by
  refine ⟨{0}, by simp, ?_⟩
  simp

/-- The **Voronoi conjecture** in dimension $d$: for every parallelohedron $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$
there exist a full-rank lattice $\Lambda \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and an affine transformation
$\mathcal{A}$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$ such that $\mathcal{A}(P)$ is the Dirichlet–Voronoi cell of
$\Lambda$. -/
def VoronoiConjectureDim (d : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ P : Set (ℝ^d), IsParallelohedron P →
    ∃ (Λ : Submodule ℤ (ℝ^d)) (_ : DiscreteTopology Λ) (_ : IsZLattice ℝ Λ) (A : ℝ^d ≃ᵃ[ℝ] ℝ^d),
      A '' P = dirichletVoronoiCell Λ

/-- **Voronoi conjecture.** Every parallelohedron, in every dimension $d$, can be mapped by an
affine transformation onto the Dirichlet–Voronoi cell of a lattice. Equivalently, every
parallelohedron is affinely equivalent to the plesiohedron obtained from a lattice. This is known
for $d \le 5$ and open for $d \ge 6$. -/
@[category research open, AMS 52]
theorem in_parallelohedron.parts.ii (d : ℕ) : VoronoiConjectureDim d := by
  sorry

/-- The three-dimensional case of the Voronoi conjecture: every parallelohedron can be made into a
plesiohedron, i.e. the Dirichlet–Voronoi cell of a lattice, by an affine transformation.
Proved by Delaunay in 1929. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 52]
theorem in_parallelohedron.parts.ii.variants.dim_three : VoronoiConjectureDim 3 := by
  sorry

/-- The four-dimensional case of the Voronoi conjecture, proved by Delaunay in 1929. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 52]
theorem in_parallelohedron.parts.ii.variants.dim_four : VoronoiConjectureDim 4 := by
  sorry

/-- The five-dimensional case of the Voronoi conjecture, proved by Garber
([arXiv:1906.05193](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.05193)). -/
@[category research solved, AMS 52]
theorem in_parallelohedron.parts.ii.variants.dim_five : VoronoiConjectureDim 5 := by
  sorry

/-- The Voronoi conjecture is known in all dimensions $d \le 5$. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 52]
theorem in_parallelohedron.parts.ii.variants.dim_le_five (d : ℕ) (hd : d ≤ 5) :
    VoronoiConjectureDim d := by
  sorry

end InParallelohedron

items: The list entry 'In parallelohedron:' is bare; the precise statement of slot ii was taken from the article and from Garber's paper (arXiv:1906.05193, Conjecture of Voronoi): ∀ d-dimensional parallelohedron P, ∃ lattice Λ and affine transformation A with A(P) the Dirichlet–Voronoi polytope of Λ.

Ambient space is `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)` (notation `ℝ^d`), so `dist` is the Euclidean metric needed for Voronoi cells. The existing repo definition `tilesByTranslation` (FormalConjecturesForMathlib/Analysis/Fourier/SpectralSets.lean) lives on `Fin d → ℝ` (sup metric) and is measure-theoretic (a.e. cover / null overlaps), so it was not reused; a geometric definition `TilesByTranslations` (translates cover ℝ^d and have pairwise disjoint interiors) was used instead. For compact convex bodies with nonempty interior the two notions agree.

`IsParallelohedron` requires the polytope to be full-dimensional (`(interior P).Nonempty`). This encodes 'd-dimensional parallelohedron' and is essential: under the disjoint-interiors tiling definition a lower-dimensional polytope (e.g. a segment in ℝ²) vacuously 'tiles' by uncountably many translates, and the conclusion would then be false.

The tiling is not required to be face-to-face or a lattice tiling. This matches Garber's definition ('P tiles ℝ^d with translated copies'); by Venkov/McMullen the face-to-face restriction is redundant for convex polytopes.

'Affine transformation' is formalized as an affine equivalence `ℝ^d ≃ᵃ[ℝ] ℝ^d`. No generality is lost: the image must be the Voronoi cell of a full-rank lattice, which has nonempty interior, so a non-invertible affine map could never work.

A lattice is a `Submodule ℤ (ℝ^d)` that is discrete and spans ℝ^d (`IsZLattice ℝ Λ`), i.e. full rank; Garber allows translates of such lattices, but a translation is absorbed by the affine map A. The Voronoi cell is the closed cell centred at the origin `{x | ∀ l ∈ Λ, dist x 0 ≤ dist x l}`.

The main declaration quantifies over all d (the conjecture as a whole is open because d ≥ 6 is open); d = 0 is included and the statement is trivially true there. Separate `research solved` variants record the known cases d = 3, 4, 5 and d ≤ 5 as reported in the article and in Garber's paper.
AMS tag 52 (convex and discrete geometry) is used, matching Garber's MSC 52B20, 52C07.

reviewer_notes: The list entry is a bare heading; both slots were read from the linked Parallelohedron article per the decomposition table. Slot ii is the Voronoi conjecture in all dimensions (open for d ≥ 6); the literal word 'plesiohedron' is broader (Voronoi cell of any periodic point set), but the article's own characterisation (face-centre vectors perpendicular to faces) and Delaunay's theorem identify it with lattice Voronoi cells, as the table's notes prescribe. The face-to-face/lattice-tiling remark in the notes is a theorem (Venkov/McMullen), not a hypothesis, so the weaker literal hypothesis 'tiles by translations' is used, matching Garber's definition. Slot i was omitted because the source is too informal to fix a unique formal reading (polyhedron/face notion, connectivity, and 'same combinatorial structure'); the two attempts (c02, c08) disagree materially and each restricts or weakens the hypothesis class. Final file compiles with only 'declaration uses sorry' warnings.
